title: Chapter 12 Drill: Genetic, Developmental, and Child Neurology

items.stem: A 3-month-old boy has severe hypotonia, a weak suck requiring tube feeding, and almond-shaped eyes. A chromosomal microarray was reported as normal. Which test is the best next step to confirm the leading diagnosis?
options: Repeat chromosomal microarray with a higher density platform
DNA methylation analysis of the 15q11 to q13 region
items.explanation: Neonatal hypotonia with feeding failure suggests Prader-Willi syndrome. A microarray detects deletions but misses maternal uniparental disomy and imprinting defects, which together account for about a third of cases. Methylation analysis detects all three mechanisms and is the correct first confirmatory test. UBE3A sequencing evaluates Angelman syndrome. A 22q11.2 deletion causes velocardiofacial syndrome, which has a different phenotype.

items.stem: A boy born at 28 weeks has spastic diplegia, with legs more affected than arms, and a scissoring gait. Which finding is most likely on brain MRI?
options: Bilateral basal ganglia and thalamic injury
items.explanation: Spastic diplegia is the typical cerebral palsy pattern after preterm birth, caused by white matter injury near the lateral ventricles, where descending leg fibers are most medial. Basal ganglia and thalamic injury follows acute profound hypoxia in a term infant and gives dyskinetic or quadriplegic cerebral palsy. A middle cerebral artery infarct yields hemiplegia, and malformations give varied phenotypes.

items.stem: A term newborn has focal clonic seizures of the right arm on day 2 with otherwise good tone and feeding. MRI shows a left middle cerebral artery territory infarct. What is the most common long term neurologic outcome?
options: Complete recovery in nearly all affected infants
Hemiparetic cerebral palsy, with possible epilepsy
items.explanation: Perinatal arterial ischemic stroke often presents with focal seizures in an otherwise well term infant, and many survivors develop hemiparetic cerebral palsy, with a substantial fraction having epilepsy, cognitive, or language problems. Most do not recover fully. Bilateral dyskinetic palsy suggests basal ganglia injury, and a one-time infarct does not cause progressive neurodegeneration. Outcome is better than after global asphyxia but is not uniformly benign.

items.stem: A 2-year-old girl has a happy demeanor with frequent laughter, ataxic gait, absent speech, microcephaly, and seizures. Brain MRI is normal. The most common genetic mechanism underlying this syndrome is which of the following?
options: A deletion of the paternally derived chromosome 15q11 to q13 region
An expanded CGG repeat in the FMR1 gene
Deletion of maternal chromosome 15q11 to q13
A de novo loss of function variant in MECP2
items.explanation: The picture is Angelman syndrome, caused by loss of the maternal UBE3A allele, since the paternal copy is silenced by imprinting in neurons. A maternal 15q11 to q13 deletion accounts for roughly two thirds of cases. The paternal deletion produces Prader-Willi syndrome. FMR1 CGG expansion causes fragile X, and MECP2 variants cause Rett syndrome, which has regression rather than a happy, ataxic phenotype.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy has new attention problems, visual decline, and hearing difficulty. MRI shows symmetric parieto-occipital white matter lesions with a rim of contrast enhancement. Which test is most useful?
options: Plasma very long chain fatty acids
items.explanation: Cerebral X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy classically presents in school-age boys with behavioral decline and posterior predominant demyelination with an advancing enhancing rim, and elevated very long chain fatty acids from ABCD1 variants confirm it. Adrenal function should also be checked. Urine organic acids, ceruloplasmin, and oligoclonal bands target other disorders and would not explain this pattern. Early recognition matters because transplantation works only before advanced disease.

items.stem: A newborn has a lumbosacral myelomeningocele. Which associated brain malformation is most likely to be found?
items.explanation: Nearly all infants with open myelomeningocele have a Chiari II malformation, with caudal displacement of the vermis and medulla through the foramen magnum, and most develop hydrocephalus requiring shunting. Dandy-Walker malformation involves vermian hypoplasia and a posterior fossa cyst. Chiari I involves isolated tonsillar descent. Holoprosencephaly is a forebrain cleavage disorder unrelated to spinal dysraphism.

items.stem: A 14-year-old girl has a first demyelinating attack with optic neuritis and an MRI showing multiple periventricular and juxtacortical lesions, two with gadolinium enhancement. Which feature favors pediatric multiple sclerosis over a monophasic disorder?
options: Complete resolution within days without therapy
Dissemination in space and time on one MRI
items.explanation: In adolescents, multiple sclerosis follows the same criteria as adults, and simultaneous enhancing and nonenhancing lesions demonstrate dissemination in time and space, a pattern also supported by periventricular and juxtacortical involvement. Encephalopathy with fever and large deep gray lesions favors acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, and full recovery within days without treatment is not specific for either condition.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy has continuous right hand jerking that persists during sleep, progressive right hemiparesis, and cognitive decline. MRI shows progressive left hemispheric atrophy. Which treatment gives the best chance of seizure freedom?
items.explanation: Rasmussen encephalitis is a unilateral inflammatory hemispheric process producing epilepsia partialis continua, progressive hemiparesis, and atrophy, and seizures are usually drug resistant. Hemispherectomy is the only treatment that reliably stops seizures, at the cost of a fixed deficit, and is considered once deficits are established. Immunotherapy may slow progression, but antiseizure medication, steroids, and stimulation rarely achieve freedom from seizures.

items.stem: A 7-year-old girl has eight café-au-lait macules larger than 5 mm and axillary freckling. Her father has similar skin findings. Which surveillance is most appropriate for her in early childhood?
options: Annual lumbar puncture for tumor markers
Surveillance echocardiography for rhabdomyoma every year
items.explanation: These findings meet criteria for neurofibromatosis type 1, in which optic pathway gliomas develop in about 15 percent of children, mostly before age 7, so annual eye examination with visual assessment is recommended. Spinal fluid tumor markers have no role. Cardiac rhabdomyomas and renal angiomyolipomas are features of tuberous sclerosis, not neurofibromatosis type 1. Visual acuity, color vision, and disc appearance are assessed at each visit.

items.stem: A 10-year-old boy has declining school performance, clumsiness, and a vertical supranuclear gaze palsy. Examination shows splenomegaly, and he has had episodes of sudden loss of muscle tone with laughter. Which gene is most likely mutated?
items.explanation: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, splenomegaly, ataxia, cognitive decline, and gelastic cataplexy characterize Niemann-Pick disease type C, most often from NPC1 variants, with defective cholesterol trafficking; miglustat slows neurologic progression. HEXA causes Tay-Sachs disease. ABCD1 causes X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, and GBA causes Gaucher disease, which can have gaze abnormalities but not this combination. Filipin staining or genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.

items.stem: A 6-month-old boy has a head circumference at the 98th percentile that has tracked parallel to the curve since birth. His father has a large head. Development, examination, and fontanelle are normal. What is the best management?
options: Lumbar puncture to measure opening pressure
Urine organic acids and lysosomal enzyme testing
items.explanation: Benign familial macrocephaly is an autosomal dominant trait in which the head runs along a high percentile with normal development and examination, and a parent often has a large head. Observation with serial measurements is appropriate. Shunting is for progressive hydrocephalus, and lumbar puncture and metabolic testing are for abnormal growth trajectories, regression, or other red flags that are absent here.

items.stem: A 9-year-old girl has fever, headache, and then acute encephalopathy with ataxia and hemiparesis after a viral illness 2 weeks earlier. MRI shows large, poorly marginated, bilateral white matter lesions. What is the first line treatment?
items.explanation: A polyfocal encephalopathy following an infection, with large asymmetric lesions, fits acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, an immune mediated, usually monophasic demyelinating illness. High-dose intravenous steroids are first line, with immunoglobulin or plasma exchange for failures. Interferon beta is a long-term therapy for multiple sclerosis. Acyclovir is for herpes encephalitis, and observation risks avoidable disability. Most children recover well, and relapse is uncommon.

items.stem: A 3-month-old boy has rapid head growth, a tense bulging fontanelle, and persistent downward deviation of the eyes with the upper sclera visible. What best explains the eye findings?
options: Bilateral abducens nerve injury from compression at the skull base
Damage to the occipital visual cortex from ischemia
Pressure on the dorsal midbrain from a dilated third ventricle
Congenital absence of the extraocular muscles
items.explanation: The sunsetting sign in raised intracranial pressure from hydrocephalus results from compression of the pretectal and dorsal midbrain region, impairing upgaze. Abducens injury causes limited abduction with esotropia rather than loss of upgaze. Cortical visual loss does not alter eye position this way, and extraocular muscle absence is a rare congenital finding that would not present with progressive head enlargement.

items.stem: A term newborn has seizures that persist despite phenobarbital and other agents. All laboratory evaluations are normal and an EEG shows multifocal activity. Which empiric step is most appropriate?
options: A pyridoxine trial with EEG monitoring
A therapeutic trial of oral zinc supplements
Hypertonic saline infusion over several hours
A trial of high-dose vitamin C and carnitine
items.explanation: Pyridoxine dependent epilepsy from ALDH7A1 deficiency causes accumulation of piperideine 6 carboxylate, which inactivates pyridoxal phosphate, and seizures stop with pyridoxine. A supervised trial with EEG monitoring in refractory neonatal or infantile seizures is standard, since the diagnosis is treatable and delay risks developmental harm. Zinc, hypertonic saline, and vitamin C have no role in refractory neonatal seizures.

items.stem: A 2-year-old with refractory seizures, microcephaly, and a movement disorder has cerebrospinal fluid glucose of 28 mg per dL with a normal serum glucose and low lactate. Which treatment is most appropriate?
items.explanation: A low cerebrospinal fluid glucose with a low CSF to blood glucose ratio and normal lactate indicates GLUT1 deficiency from SLC2A1 variants, which impairs glucose transport into the brain. Ketones provide an alternative cerebral fuel, so a ketogenic diet is the treatment of choice and seizures often resolve. Carbohydrate loading does not cross the transporter, and pyridoxine and immunoglobulin do not fix the transport defect.

items.stem: A 10-year-old boy has growth failure, headaches, and bitemporal hemianopia. CT shows a suprasellar cystic mass with calcification. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanation: A calcified, cystic suprasellar mass compressing the optic chiasm and pituitary stalk, with growth failure and visual field loss, is typical of craniopharyngioma, derived from remnants of Rathke pouch. The other tumors arise in the posterior fossa and would not produce bitemporal field loss or endocrine dysfunction from a sellar region mass. Endocrine replacement is often needed after treatment.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man has MELAS with a confirmed pathogenic mitochondrial DNA point variant. He and his healthy wife ask about the risk to their future children. What is the most accurate counseling statement?
options: All of his daughters will inherit the variant through his X chromosome
Half of his sons will be affected, as in X-linked recessive disease
Each child has a one in four risk, as in autosomal recessive disease
None of his children will inherit it, as mitochondrial DNA is maternal
items.explanation: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited almost exclusively through the oocyte cytoplasm, so a father does not pass his variant to any child. A mother with a heteroplasmic variant can transmit it to all children, with variable severity. The pattern does not follow X-linked or autosomal recessive ratios, so quoting a fixed fraction of sons, daughters, or a one in four risk misapplies Mendelian rules.

items.stem: A 4-year-old boy has progressive ataxia, conjunctival telangiectasias, and frequent sinopulmonary infections. Which laboratory finding best supports the diagnosis?
options: Elevated very long chain fatty acids
items.explanation: Ataxia-telangiectasia is an autosomal recessive DNA repair disorder from ATM variants, with cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, immunodeficiency, radiosensitivity, and lymphoid malignancy risk. Elevated alpha-fetoprotein is characteristic. Low ceruloplasmin suggests Wilson disease, high very long chain fatty acids suggest adrenoleukodystrophy, and low vitamin E causes ataxia with vitamin E deficiency. Radiation exposure from imaging is minimized because of cellular radiosensitivity.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy with autism has severe irritability with aggression. After behavioral measures fail, risperidone is started. Which adverse effect should be monitored most closely?
options: Hepatic failure within the first month
Pancreatitis from hypertriglyceridemia in all patients
items.explanation: Risperidone is approved for irritability associated with autism, and its main adverse effects are weight gain, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, hyperprolactinemia, and extrapyramidal symptoms, so weight, glucose, lipids, and prolactin related symptoms are monitored. Agranulocytosis is the concern with clozapine. Hepatic failure and pancreatitis are not characteristic of this drug, and neither requires routine surveillance of every patient.

items.stem: An 18-month-old girl has chaotic multidirectional eye movements, jerking of the limbs, and ataxia, and she is irritable. Which evaluation is most important?
options: Plain skull radiographs to look for fracture
Lumbar puncture for bacterial culture only
items.explanation: Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome in toddlers is a paraneoplastic or postinfectious immune disorder, and about half have neuroblastoma, so urine catecholamines and chest and abdominal imaging are needed, often with MIBG scanning. Skull radiographs and hearing tests have no relevance. A culture-only lumbar puncture will not identify the tumor that drives the immune mechanism. Immunotherapy is then started alongside tumor treatment.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman has progressive bilateral hearing loss and tinnitus. MRI shows bilateral enhancing masses in the internal auditory canals, and her mother had similar findings. Which chromosome and gene are most likely involved?
options: VHL on chromosome 3, encoding the VHL protein
items.explanation: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are diagnostic of neurofibromatosis type 2, an autosomal dominant disorder from NF2 variants on chromosome 22 producing the tumor suppressor merlin. NF1 on chromosome 17 causes the cutaneous and peripheral nerve phenotype. VHL on chromosome 3 causes hemangioblastomas and renal tumors, and TSC2 on chromosome 16 causes tuberous sclerosis. Genetic counseling is offered to relatives who may carry the same variant.

items.stem: A 3-year-old boy has a unilateral facial capillary malformation involving the forehead and upper eyelid, focal seizures, and mild hemiparesis. Which ophthalmologic complication needs routine screening?
items.explanation: Sturge-Weber syndrome, caused by mosaic GNAQ variants, combines a facial capillary malformation in the ophthalmic distribution with leptomeningeal angiomatosis, seizures, and glaucoma, which can be congenital or develop later and needs regular pressure checks. Retinoblastoma, Lisch nodules, and optic glioma belong to other syndromes and do not result from this vascular malformation. Early glaucoma control and seizure management protect long term function.

items.stem: A 5-year-old boy is being evaluated for neurofibromatosis type 2 because his mother has bilateral vestibular schwannomas. Which ocular finding would support the diagnosis in him?
options: Retinal capillary hemangioma of the fundus
items.explanation: Juvenile posterior subcapsular cataract is a common early ocular manifestation of neurofibromatosis type 2 and may precede tumors. Lisch nodules are iris hamartomas of neurofibromatosis type 1. Retinal capillary hemangiomas occur in von Hippel-Lindau disease, and angioid streaks occur in pseudoxanthoma elasticum, so they would not support this diagnosis. Slit lamp examination is therefore part of presymptomatic assessment.

items.stem: A pediatrician wants to use a validated screening tool for autism spectrum disorder at routine well visits. At which ages is universal screening recommended?
options: At birth and 6 months with a reflex checklist
At 18 and 24 months using the M-CHAT-R/F
At age 4 years and at school entry only
items.explanation: Guidelines recommend developmental surveillance at every visit and autism specific screening with a validated tool at 18 and 24 months, with general developmental screening at 9, 18, and 30 months. Screening is universal and not limited to children with parental concern. Reflex checklists at birth do not detect autism, and waiting until school entry delays early intervention, which improves outcomes.

items.stem: A woman is a known carrier of an X-linked recessive neurologic disorder, and her partner is unaffected. She is pregnant and asks about inheritance. What risk applies to each pregnancy?
options: All sons are affected and all daughters are carriers
A quarter of all children are affected
No son is affected and half of daughters are affected
Half of sons affected, half of daughters carriers
items.explanation: A carrier mother passes the abnormal X to each child with a probability of one half. A son who receives it is affected because he has no second X, and a daughter who receives it is usually an unaffected carrier. All sons or all daughters would require an affected father or homozygous mother, and the autosomal recessive one in four figure does not apply. Daughters are rarely affected.

items.stem: A term newborn has repeated focal clonic seizures at 20 hours of age, with documented hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy and a normal glucose and electrolytes. Which medication is the preferred first line antiseizure drug?
items.explanation: Phenobarbital remains the first line agent for neonatal seizures after metabolic causes are excluded, based on its efficacy and extensive neonatal experience, with levetiracetam or phenytoin as second line options. Carbamazepine has no intravenous formulation and is not used for acute neonatal seizures. Valproic acid carries a risk of hepatotoxicity and metabolic disease unmasking in infancy.

items.stem: A 3-year-old boy has global developmental delay and no dysmorphic features, no seizures, and a normal examination apart from delay. Metabolic screening is unremarkable. Which genetic test is recommended as the first tier evaluation?
options: Targeted sequencing of a single gene such as MECP2
items.explanation: Chromosomal microarray has the highest diagnostic yield among first tier tests for unexplained global developmental delay, intellectual disability, or autism, detecting copy number variants that a karyotype cannot resolve. Fragile X testing is added in boys, and exome sequencing is increasingly used as an equal or next step. Single gene sequencing is low yield without a recognizable phenotype, and mitochondrial sequencing needs supporting clinical features.

items.stem: A 4-month-old infant has seizures, hypotonia, eczematous rash, and thinning hair. Urine organic acids show 3-hydroxyisovalerate and lactate. Which treatment is appropriate?
options: Riboflavin together with a ketogenic diet
items.explanation: Biotinidase deficiency impairs recycling of biotin, causing multiple carboxylase deficiency, with seizures, hypotonia, alopecia, skin rash, and organic aciduria. It is detected on newborn screening and fully treatable with pharmacologic doses of biotin for life, which prevents hearing loss, optic atrophy, and developmental impairment. Thiamine, protein restriction alone, or riboflavin with ketosis do not correct this enzyme defect.

items.stem: A 6-year-old with spastic cerebral palsy walks with a toe-walking pattern. Examination shows focal gastrocnemius spasticity with a mobile ankle joint and no fixed contracture. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Placement of an intrathecal baclofen pump
Surgical tendon transfer at the hip
Botulinum toxin into the calf muscles
items.explanation: Focal muscle overactivity with a dynamic equinus is best treated with intramuscular botulinum toxin, usually combined with stretching, bracing, and therapy. Intrathecal baclofen is reserved for severe generalized spasticity or dystonia. Hip procedures are for hip displacement, and chronic benzodiazepine use causes sedation and tolerance without functional benefit for localized spasticity. Injection is repeated about every three to six months as needed.

items.stem: An 8-month-old boy has a persistent asymmetric tonic neck reflex, has not rolled over, and has increased tone in the legs. What is the best interpretation of the retained primitive reflex?
options: It is a normal finding that fades by 12 months
It indicates a peripheral neuropathy of infancy
It confirms benign congenital hypotonia of infancy
Upper motor neuron injury such as cerebral palsy
items.explanation: Primitive reflexes such as the asymmetric tonic neck reflex normally fade by about 4 to 6 months, and persistence beyond that age with hypertonia and motor delay indicates a corticospinal injury, typically cerebral palsy. A normal reflex would not remain obligatory at eight months. Peripheral neuropathy gives hypotonia with absent reflexes, and benign congenital hypotonia does not produce increased tone.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy has choreoathetosis, sensorineural hearing loss, and limited upgaze. He had severe neonatal jaundice that was not treated promptly. Which structure is most characteristically injured by this process?
items.explanation: Bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus) deposits unconjugated bilirubin preferentially in the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, and brainstem auditory nuclei, giving dyskinetic cerebral palsy, hearing loss, and upgaze palsy. Caudate head, vermis, and occipital cortex are not the typical targets, and the combination of dystonia, deafness, and gaze impairment points to this basal ganglia and brainstem pattern. Phototherapy and exchange transfusion prevent the injury in the neonatal period.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy has bilateral optic neuritis with long optic nerve involvement and perineural enhancement. Serum aquaporin-4 antibody is negative. Which test is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanation: Pediatric optic neuritis with bilateral, long segment, perineural involvement is characteristic of myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease, which is more common in children than aquaporin-4 disease. A live cell-based assay on serum is the recommended test. Oligoclonal bands are less frequent in this disorder and are not a serum test. Biopsy is unnecessary, and ceruloplasmin addresses Wilson disease.

items.stem: A 5-year-old previously verbal girl progressively loses comprehension of spoken language over several months and becomes mute. She has occasional seizures. A sleep EEG shows near continuous bilateral spike and wave activity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanation: Acquired epileptic aphasia in a previously normal child, with auditory agnosia and electrical status epilepticus during slow sleep, defines Landau-Kleffner syndrome. Childhood disintegrative disorder involves broad regression of social, motor, and language skills without this EEG pattern. Rett syndrome involves hand stereotypies in girls under 2 years, and Lennox-Gastaut features multiple seizure types, slow spike-wave, and cognitive impairment.

items.stem: A 5-year-old girl is inattentive, restless, and impulsive in both preschool and at home, with significant impairment. She has no tics or cardiac history. According to pediatric guidelines, what is the preferred first treatment?
options: Immediate treatment with a long-acting stimulant
Referral for a trial of risperidone
items.explanation: For children aged 4 to 5 years with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, behavioral parent training is the first line, and methylphenidate is considered only if behavioral treatment fails and symptoms remain moderate to severe. Atomoxetine and antipsychotics are not first line, and risperidone carries metabolic risk that is unjustified here. Behavioral therapy is also valuable alongside medication in older children.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man with Down syndrome develops progressive memory loss, new myoclonic jerks, and a first generalized seizure. His baseline function had been stable for decades. Which mechanism best explains this early dementia?
options: Triplication of the APP gene on chromosome 21
Expanded polyglutamine repeat in the huntingtin protein
Loss of the maternal UBE3A allele
items.explanation: People with trisomy 21 carry three copies of APP, which increases amyloid beta production, so Alzheimer neuropathology is nearly universal by middle age and clinical dementia often starts in the forties or fifties. Late onset myoclonus and seizures are common. Huntingtin repeats cause Huntington disease, UBE3A loss causes Angelman syndrome, and mitochondrial variants cause other encephalopathies, none of which fit this chromosomal context.

items.stem: A 4-year-old girl has progressive visual loss, myoclonic and tonic-clonic seizures, ataxia, and loss of language. EEG shows a posterior spike response to low-frequency photic stimulation. Which treatment is specific for the most likely form of this disease?
options: Intravenous thiamine for pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency
items.explanation: Late infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN2) presents with seizures, vision loss, and regression, and the electroretinogram and photic response at slow flash rates are helpful clues. Cerliponase alfa, an enzyme replacement therapy delivered into the ventricles, slows decline in tripeptidyl peptidase 1 deficiency. Miglustat addresses Niemann-Pick C and Gaucher disease, and thiamine and biotin treat distinct metabolic defects.

items.stem: A 6-day-old infant feeds poorly, has alternating hypertonia and hypotonia, and has urine and cerumen with a sweet maple syrup odor. Which amino acid is most elevated in plasma?
items.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease arises from deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, so leucine, isoleucine, and valine accumulate, and leucine and its ketoacid are chiefly neurotoxic, causing encephalopathy with cerebral edema. Phenylalanine is raised in phenylketonuria, methionine in homocystinuria or methionine adenosyltransferase deficiency, and glycine in nonketotic hyperglycinemia. Treatment includes a leucine restricted diet and dialysis in crisis.

items.stem: A woman who previously gave birth to a child with a neural tube defect is planning another pregnancy. What is the recommended folic acid supplementation?
options: Folic acid 4 mg daily, starting a month before conception
Folic acid 400 micrograms daily, begun after the first trimester
items.explanation: Women with a prior pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect should take 4 mg of folic acid daily beginning at least a month before conception and through early pregnancy, which lowers recurrence by roughly 70 percent. Standard 400 microgram supplementation is for the general population and should begin before conception, not after the first trimester. B12 injections do not substitute for folate.

items.stem: A 10-year-old boy with tuberous sclerosis has a growing subependymal giant cell astrocytoma at the foramen of Monro with early ventricular enlargement. Which medical therapy is approved for this tumor?
items.explanation: Tuberous sclerosis results from TSC1 or TSC2 loss, which disinhibits mTOR signaling, and the mTOR inhibitor everolimus shrinks subependymal giant cell astrocytomas and renal angiomyolipomas, and reduces seizures in some patients. Selumetinib targets the MEK pathway in neurofibromatosis type 1. Temozolomide and bevacizumab are not established treatments for this slow growing, benign tumor. Common adverse effects include mouth ulcers and hyperlipidemia.

items.stem: A 4-month-old girl is alert and socially responsive but lies in a frog-leg posture with a bell-shaped chest. She has absent deep tendon reflexes, tongue fasciculations, and paradoxical breathing. Which test is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Muscle biopsy with dystrophin staining of fibers
Testing for SMN1 deletion with SMN2 copy number
items.explanation: Alert hypotonia with areflexia, tongue fasciculations, and a bell-shaped chest points to spinal muscular atrophy type 1, confirmed by homozygous SMN1 deletion; SMN2 copy number predicts severity and guides therapy. Dystrophin staining evaluates Duchenne dystrophy, which does not present with areflexia in infancy. MRI and spinal fluid analysis are not expected to be informative, since the lesion is in the anterior horn cell.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man has headaches and ataxia. MRI shows a cystic cerebellar mass with an enhancing mural nodule, and fundoscopy shows a retinal capillary angioma. Which additional screening is most important?
options: Skin biopsy for fibroblast enzyme studies
items.explanation: Cerebellar hemangioblastoma with retinal hemangioblastoma indicates von Hippel-Lindau disease, from VHL tumor suppressor loss on chromosome 3, which predisposes to clear cell renal carcinoma and pheochromocytoma, so renal imaging and metanephrines are required. Alpha-fetoprotein and immunoglobulins relate to ataxia-telangiectasia, rhabdomyomas to tuberous sclerosis, and fibroblast enzymes to lysosomal diseases. Lifelong surveillance with imaging is required because new lesions continue to appear.

items.stem: An infant born small for gestational age has microcephaly, petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, and failed newborn hearing screening. Head ultrasound shows periventricular calcifications. Which congenital infection is most likely?
items.explanation: Periventricular calcifications with microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss, and thrombocytopenia with hepatosplenomegaly are typical of congenital cytomegalovirus, the most common congenital infection. Toxoplasmosis produces scattered calcifications with hydrocephalus and chorioretinitis. Rubella causes cataracts and cardiac defects, and congenital herpes more often presents with vesicles, encephalitis, and cortical or temporal lobe injury. Valganciclovir is considered for symptomatic central nervous system disease.

items.stem: A premature infant born at 27 weeks develops apnea, bulging fontanelle, and a falling hematocrit on day 3. Cranial ultrasound shows blood within the ventricles. Where does this hemorrhage typically originate?
options: The choroid plexus of the third ventricle
The subarachnoid space over the convexities
The germinal matrix at the caudothalamic groove
items.explanation: Intraventricular hemorrhage in preterm infants arises from the fragile, richly vascularized germinal matrix near the caudothalamic groove, which involutes by term. Autoregulation is poor in these infants, so fluctuations in blood pressure rupture the vessels. Choroid plexus bleeding is more typical of term infants, subarachnoid hemorrhage has other causes, and cerebellar hemorrhage is less common in this setting.

items.stem: A 26-month-old boy has about ten single words and no two-word phrases. He plays appropriately, makes good eye contact, and follows simple commands. What is the most appropriate first step in his evaluation?
items.explanation: Failure to combine words by 24 months is a red flag for language delay, and hearing loss is a common, treatable cause that must be excluded first. Preserved social engagement and comprehension make autism less likely. MRI, sleep EEG, and genetic testing are reserved for children with additional findings such as regression, seizures, dysmorphism, or global delay, and should not precede hearing assessment.

items.stem: A newborn is profoundly hypotonic with facial diplegia, a tented upper lip, and respiratory failure needing ventilation. Her mother has had weakness and difficulty relaxing her grip for years. Which genetic event is most likely in this infant?
options: Paternal transmission of a deletion at 15q11 to q13
Deletion of the SMN1 gene on both alleles
Maternal transmission of a large CTG expansion
Loss of the maternal UBE3A allele
items.explanation: Congenital myotonic dystrophy type 1 occurs almost only with maternal transmission of a large CTG expansion, which shows marked anticipation. Neonates have hypotonia, facial weakness, feeding difficulty, and respiratory failure, and the mother often has undiagnosed myotonia. Paternal 15q deletion leads to Prader-Willi syndrome without the maternal history. SMN1 deletion gives spinal muscular atrophy with areflexia, and UBE3A loss causes Angelman syndrome.

items.stem: A term infant has a jittery appearance and a seizure at 24 hours after birth. Bedside glucose is 18 mg per dL. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Intravenous dextrose bolus then continuous infusion
Oral feeding with formula and recheck in a few hours
items.explanation: Symptomatic neonatal hypoglycemia is a neurologic emergency, and prompt intravenous dextrose bolus followed by a maintenance infusion prevents permanent brain injury. Phenobarbital alone does not correct the cause. Feeds are not adequate when seizures or severe hypoglycemia are present, and lumbar puncture should not delay glucose correction, though infection may be evaluated afterward. Glucose is then rechecked frequently until it is stable.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl has steadily worsening unsteadiness of gait with areflexia at the ankles, upgoing toes, scoliosis, and pes cavus. An echocardiogram shows concentric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Which genetic test is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
options: Analysis for a CAG repeat expansion in ATXN1
Analysis for a CTG repeat expansion in DMPK
Testing for a GAA expansion in FXN
items.explanation: Friedreich ataxia is the most common recessively inherited ataxia and results from a homozygous GAA expansion in the frataxin gene, causing mitochondrial iron accumulation. Areflexia with upgoing toes, scoliosis, and cardiomyopathy are typical. ATXN1 CAG expansion causes dominant spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 in adults. ATM variants cause ataxia-telangiectasia with telangiectasias. DMPK CTG expansion causes myotonic dystrophy.

items.stem: A boy with X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy has early cerebral MRI changes with a low Loes score but is still neurologically intact. Which intervention gives the best chance of halting progression?
items.explanation: In cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, or autologous gene therapy where available, can arrest demyelination only when performed early, before significant neurologic deficit and while MRI involvement is limited. Corticosteroids treat the adrenal insufficiency but not the leukodystrophy. Plasma exchange and baclofen do not alter disease course and are not disease modifying. Adrenal insufficiency is managed separately with replacement steroids.

items.stem: A 2-year-old child has gait regression, peripheral neuropathy with slowed nerve conduction, and diffuse leukodystrophy on MRI. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely?
items.explanation: Metachromatic leukodystrophy, caused by arylsulfatase A deficiency and sulfatide accumulation, causes a demyelinating neuropathy together with central white matter disease and gait regression in toddlers. Galactocerebrosidase deficiency (Krabbe disease) usually presents earlier with irritability and hypertonia. Hexosaminidase A deficiency produces gray matter disease, and alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease with pain and vascular events.

items.stem: A female infant has a linear vesicular rash on the limbs that evolves into verrucous lesions and then swirled hyperpigmentation, with seizures at 3 weeks of age. Her mother has patchy dental abnormalities. What is the most likely inheritance pattern?
options: Autosomal recessive with equal risk in both sexes
Autosomal dominant with full penetrance in males
X-linked dominant, usually lethal in males
items.explanation: The evolving skin stages along Blaschko lines with seizures and dental anomalies describe incontinentia pigmenti, caused by IKBKG variants and inherited as an X-linked dominant trait that is typically lethal in hemizygous males. Hypomelanosis of Ito has hypopigmented swirls without these stages. Autosomal recessive or mitochondrial inheritance would not explain female predominance, and males are rarely survivors.

items.stem: A 5-year-old girl has recurrent episodes of transient hemiparesis triggered by crying and hyperventilation. Angiography shows bilateral terminal internal carotid stenosis with a puff of smoke collateral pattern. What is the most effective long term treatment?
items.explanation: Moyamoya arteriopathy with symptoms provoked by hyperventilation reflects hemodynamic ischemia from progressive stenosis. Direct or indirect revascularization surgery lowers recurrent stroke risk, and aspirin is often added. Warfarin is not established, thrombolysis is not given for transient events, and carbamazepine treats focal seizures but not the underlying ischemia. Avoiding hyperventilation and dehydration lowers the chance of an event.

items.stem: A prenatal ultrasound shows multiple cardiac rhabdomyomas in a fetus. After birth, which condition should be suspected, and what is the appropriate next evaluation?
options: Neurofibromatosis type 1, with optic nerve imaging only
Tuberous sclerosis complex, with brain MRI and EEG
items.explanation: Cardiac rhabdomyomas, especially multiple, are present in most infants with tuberous sclerosis and often detected prenatally, so brain MRI for tubers and subependymal nodules, EEG for epileptiform activity, and genetic testing are appropriate. Neurofibromatosis type 1 does not produce rhabdomyomas. Sturge-Weber causes facial capillary malformation and glaucoma, and ataxia-telangiectasia causes ataxia and immune deficiency later in childhood.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man with neurofibromatosis type 1 reports rapid growth and new severe pain in a long-standing plexiform neurofibroma of the thigh. What is the most likely concern?
options: Benign enlargement that needs only reassurance
Optic pathway glioma with local invasion
items.explanation: Plexiform neurofibromas carry a lifetime risk of malignant transformation of about 10 percent, and rapid growth, new pain, or neurologic deficit suggests malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor, so FDG-PET and biopsy are needed. Reassurance would delay care. Optic pathway glioma arises in the visual pathway, and vestibular schwannoma is a feature of neurofibromatosis type 2 rather than a thigh lesion.

items.stem: A term newborn has an Apgar score of 2 at 10 minutes, cord arterial pH of 6.9, and then develops lethargy, hypotonia, and seizures within the first hours. What is the most appropriate neuroprotective treatment?
options: Prophylactic high-dose phenobarbital given without therapeutic cooling
Whole-body cooling to 33.5 C for 72 hours, begun within 6 hours
Observation until MRI is obtained at one week
items.explanation: Moderate to severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy in a term infant is treated with therapeutic hypothermia, which reduces death and disability when begun within 6 hours and maintained for 72 hours. Prophylactic barbiturates and corticosteroids have not improved outcome and corticosteroids do not treat cytotoxic edema. Waiting for MRI wastes the narrow treatment window. Cooling is continued with rewarming over several hours afterward.

items.stem: A 5-year-old boy has an elongated face, prominent ears, joint hyperextensibility, language delay, and hand flapping with poor eye contact. His maternal uncle has intellectual disability. Which test is most appropriate to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
options: Methylation analysis of chromosome 15q11 to q13
DNA analysis of the CGG repeat number in FMR1
items.explanation: Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and a leading single gene cause of autism. Diagnosis rests on molecular analysis of CGG repeats in FMR1, with a full mutation above 200 repeats and hypermethylation. A karyotype rarely shows the fragile site anymore. MECP2 sequencing evaluates Rett syndrome, and 15q11 to q13 methylation evaluates Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes.

items.stem: An 8-year-old boy has a sudden onset of obsessive-compulsive symptoms and motor tics two weeks after confirmed streptococcal pharyngitis. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Treat documented infection and use standard OCD therapy
Start long-term antibiotic prophylaxis for every patient indefinitely
Begin immunoglobulin infusions in every patient
Perform tonsillectomy to cure the disorder
items.explanation: The proposed link between streptococcal infection and abrupt onset obsessive-compulsive symptoms (PANDAS) remains controversial, and evidence does not support routine immunotherapy, tonsillectomy, or routine prophylaxis. Documented active infection is treated, and the symptoms receive cognitive behavioral therapy and, when needed, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Immunomodulation is considered only within a research or specialist framework.

items.stem: A 4-year-old boy has difficulty climbing stairs, uses his hands to push up from the floor, and has enlarged calves. Creatine kinase is 18,000 units per liter. What is the most appropriate confirmatory test?
options: Needle electromyography as the first confirmatory test
Brain MRI to look for white matter changes
Nerve conduction study of the legs
items.explanation: This is the classic presentation of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, with a Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, and markedly raised creatine kinase. Deletion and duplication testing of the dystrophin gene confirms about two thirds of cases, followed by sequencing if negative, and muscle biopsy is now rarely needed. Electromyography and nerve conduction are nonspecific, and brain MRI does not address a primary muscle disease.

items.stem: A 5-year-old girl has diplopia, facial asymmetry, gait ataxia, and long tract signs over three weeks. MRI shows diffuse expansion of the pons with little enhancement. What is the standard treatment?
items.explanation: Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma presents with rapidly progressive cranial neuropathies, ataxia, and long tract signs, and its infiltrative growth makes resection impossible and biopsy rarely necessary. Radiation gives temporary improvement and remains standard care, though prognosis is poor. Surgery cannot remove an infiltrating brainstem tumor, methotrexate has no established role, and observation forfeits the only effective palliation.

items.stem: A 5-month-old infant with hypopigmented macules has episodes of clustered flexion of the trunk and arms, and EEG shows hypsarrhythmia. Which treatment is preferred for the spasms?
items.explanation: Infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis respond best to vigabatrin, which inhibits GABA transaminase and is first line in this setting, with adrenocorticotropic hormone as an alternative. Visual field loss is a recognized risk requiring monitoring. Carbamazepine and phenytoin can aggravate infantile spasms or fail to control them, and ethosuximide targets absence seizures, not this epileptic encephalopathy.

items.stem: A 4-month-old infant is irritable and hypertonic, with optic atrophy and episodic fevers without infection. Cerebrospinal fluid protein is elevated and MRI shows involvement of the corticospinal tracts and cerebellar white matter. What is the underlying defect?
options: Arylsulfatase A deficiency with sulfatide accumulation
Frataxin deficiency with mitochondrial iron overload
Hexosaminidase B deficiency with globoside accumulation
items.explanation: Krabbe disease presents in early infancy with irritability, stiffness, optic atrophy, and hyperproteinorachia, and the neurotoxic metabolite psychosine causes oligodendrocyte death and globoid cells; newborn screening permits early transplantation. Sulfatide accumulation defines metachromatic leukodystrophy, which presents later. Frataxin deficiency causes Friedreich ataxia, and hexosaminidase B deficiency is part of Sandhoff disease with a cherry-red spot.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy has persistent inattention and impulsivity at school and home, confirmed by parent and teacher rating scales. Hearing, vision, and sleep are normal. What is the preferred treatment approach?
options: An atypical antipsychotic as first line therapy
items.explanation: For school-age children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, stimulant medication such as methylphenidate or amphetamine, together with behavioral interventions, is first line and has the strongest evidence for core symptoms. Deferring treatment risks academic and social harm. Antidepressants are not effective as monotherapy, and antipsychotics are reserved for comorbid aggression or refractory problems, not as first line therapy.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man has been diagnosed with Huntington disease. His 14-year-old nephew carries the expanded CAG repeat and has a repeat length much larger than the proband's. The nephew inherited the allele from his father, who is the proband's brother. Which transmission feature explains the larger expansion?
options: Expansion is more likely during maternal transmission
Expansion occurs only in somatic cells of the child
Expansion is likelier through the father
items.explanation: In Huntington disease the CAG repeat tends to lengthen when passed through the male germline, producing anticipation with earlier onset in children of affected fathers. Maternal transmission usually shows little change, as in fragile X where the maternal route drives expansion. The expansion is a germline event, not somatic only, and the disorder is nuclear, so mitochondrial heteroplasmy is irrelevant.

items.stem: A 10-day-old infant has a vesicular skin lesion, fever, and focal seizures. Cerebrospinal fluid shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis and red blood cells. Which treatment should be started immediately?
items.explanation: Neonatal herpes simplex encephalitis acquired at delivery presents in the first weeks with vesicles, fever, and seizures, and mortality is high without early therapy. Empiric intravenous acyclovir is started at once, before confirmation by CSF polymerase chain reaction. Ceftriaxone does not cover the virus and should not be given to neonates with jaundice. Corticosteroids are not treatment, and fluconazole targets fungal infection.

items.stem: A 5-month-old infant has constipation, weak cry, poor suck, ptosis, and descending symmetric weakness over several days. Her parents have been giving a home remedy of raw honey. What is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanation: Infant botulism results from ingestion of Clostridium botulinum spores, which colonize the gut and release toxin, causing descending cranial and limb weakness after constipation. Human-derived botulism immune globulin shortens illness and hospitalization and is given as soon as diagnosis is suspected. Antibiotics are not needed and aminoglycosides can worsen blockade. Pyridostigmine and plasma exchange are not effective.

items.stem: A parent asks what is required to make the diagnosis of intellectual disability in her 9-year-old son, who scored 65 on a standardized intelligence test. Which additional criterion is essential?
options: Impaired adaptive functioning from early life
A structural abnormality found on neuroimaging
A positive result on a diagnostic genetic test
items.explanation: Diagnosis requires deficits in intellectual functioning, roughly two standard deviations below the mean, plus deficits in adaptive functioning across conceptual, social, and practical domains, with onset in the developmental period. Imaging abnormalities, regression, or a genetic diagnosis may help find a cause but are not required, and many children have no identifiable structural or genetic abnormality.

items.stem: A 12-day-old infant has fever, poor feeding, and lethargy. Which organism requires specific coverage with ampicillin in empiric treatment of bacterial meningitis at this age?
items.explanation: Neonatal meningitis is caused mainly by group B streptococcus and Escherichia coli, with Listeria monocytogenes an important cause that cephalosporins do not cover, so ampicillin is included in empiric regimens in this age group. Meningococcus, Haemophilus, and pneumococcus are leading causes beyond the neonatal period, and vaccination has greatly lowered Haemophilus disease. Gentamicin or cefotaxime is added for gram-negative coverage.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy with neurofibromatosis type 1 has a large inoperable plexiform neurofibroma of the face causing airway compromise and disfigurement. Which drug class is approved for this indication?
options: An mTOR inhibitor such as everolimus
A MEK inhibitor such as selumetinib
A calcineurin inhibitor such as tacrolimus
items.explanation: Neurofibromin loss activates RAS and the downstream MEK pathway, and the MEK inhibitor selumetinib is approved for children with symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibromas, producing tumor volume reduction in most. Everolimus is used for tuberous sclerosis, where TSC1 and TSC2 loss activates mTOR. Proton pump inhibitors and calcineurin inhibitors do not target the tumor biology. It is given orally, and cardiac function and skin toxicity are monitored.

items.stem: A girl develops normally until 12 months, then loses purposeful hand use, develops constant hand wringing, and shows deceleration of head growth with episodes of breath holding. She later has seizures and gait apraxia. A pathogenic variant in which gene is most likely?
items.explanation: Classic Rett syndrome is an X-linked disorder due to MECP2 variants, almost exclusively in girls because affected males usually die early. The sequence of normal early development, regression of hand skills and speech, stereotypic hand wringing, and acquired microcephaly is characteristic. UBE3A is the Angelman gene. FMR1 causes fragile X. CDKL5 variants cause early onset refractory epilepsy rather than regression after a normal first year.

items.stem: A 3-day-old term infant becomes lethargic and tachypneic after starting feeds. Ammonia is markedly elevated, blood gas shows respiratory alkalosis, and glucose is normal. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Stop protein, give intravenous glucose, start nitrogen scavengers
Give intravenous antibiotics for presumed sepsis and continue feeds
Start high-dose phenobarbital for presumed seizures
items.explanation: Neonatal hyperammonemia with respiratory alkalosis suggests a urea cycle disorder such as ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency. Treatment is to halt protein catabolism and intake, supply calories as intravenous glucose, and give sodium benzoate and phenylacetate, with dialysis for severe or refractory cases. Continuing protein worsens ammonia. Phenobarbital does not address the cause, and a ketogenic formula supplies fat but does not treat the block.

items.stem: A 9-month-old infant has regression, hypotonia, vomiting, and lactic acidosis. MRI shows bilateral symmetric T2 hyperintensities in the basal ganglia and brainstem. Which diagnosis best fits?
items.explanation: Subacute necrotizing encephalomyelopathy (Leigh syndrome) is a mitochondrial disorder, often from SURF1 or other respiratory chain variants, with developmental regression, lactic acidosis, and symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem lesions. Kernicterus follows severe hyperbilirubinemia in the neonatal period and involves the globus pallidus. Wilson disease does not present in infancy, and hypoglycemic injury favors the parieto-occipital cortex.

items.stem: Two siblings share the same pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variant inherited from their mother. One has mild migraine and hearing loss, while the other has stroke-like episodes and lactic acidosis. What best explains this variability?
options: Different parental origin of the nuclear alleles at imprinted loci
Variable CAG repeat length between the two siblings
Different mutant mtDNA loads in affected tissues
Skewed X inactivation in the female sibling only
items.explanation: Cells contain many mitochondrial genomes, so mutant and normal copies coexist (heteroplasmy). Phenotype appears when the mutant load in a tissue exceeds a threshold, and the load can differ between siblings and organs because of random segregation of mitochondria. Imprinting concerns nuclear genes, trinucleotide repeat length is a nuclear mechanism, and X inactivation cannot explain the problem if both siblings are not female.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has no neurologic symptoms. Transcranial Doppler shows a time-averaged maximum mean velocity of 220 cm per second in the middle cerebral artery on two occasions. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Observation with repeat Doppler in 5 years
items.explanation: Velocities of 200 cm per second or above on transcranial Doppler identify children at high risk of first ischemic stroke, and regular transfusions to keep hemoglobin S low reduced stroke risk by about 90 percent in a landmark trial. Aspirin has not been shown to give equivalent protection. Waiting years risks stroke, and endarterectomy is not used in this intracranial small-vessel setting.

items.stem: A 9-year-old girl has headaches and a unilateral cerebellar cyst with a small enhancing mural nodule. Which histologic feature is most characteristic of this tumor?
items.explanation: A cystic cerebellar mass with an enhancing nodule in a child is classically a pilocytic astrocytoma, a WHO grade 1 tumor with a very good prognosis after complete resection, and its histology shows biphasic architecture with Rosenthal fibers and eosinophilic granular bodies. Homer Wright rosettes occur in medulloblastoma, perivascular pseudorosettes in ependymoma, and psammoma bodies in meningioma.

items.stem: An infant has hydrocephalus, scattered intracranial calcifications throughout the cortex and basal ganglia, and bilateral chorioretinitis. Her mother ate undercooked lamb during pregnancy. Which regimen is the recommended treatment?
options: Oral valganciclovir for six months of therapy
Intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin for 7 days
items.explanation: Congenital toxoplasmosis with the classic triad of hydrocephalus, diffuse calcifications, and chorioretinitis is treated with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine for many months, with folinic acid to prevent marrow suppression. Acyclovir treats herpes simplex disease, and valganciclovir treats symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus. Ampicillin with gentamicin covers neonatal bacterial infection and does not treat protozoal disease. Early treatment lowers the burden of eye and neurologic sequelae.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy has morning vomiting, headaches, and truncal ataxia. CT shows a hyperdense midline posterior fossa mass with obstructive hydrocephalus. Which tumor is most likely, and what is a characteristic feature?
options: Pilocytic astrocytoma, with a cyst and a mural nodule
Diffuse pontine glioma, with brainstem expansion
items.explanation: A hyperdense midline vermian mass in a young child, reflecting high cellularity, with obstructive hydrocephalus is typical of medulloblastoma, an embryonal tumor that seeds the cerebrospinal fluid and requires full neuraxis imaging. A cyst with a mural nodule describes pilocytic astrocytoma. Craniopharyngioma sits in the suprasellar region, and diffuse pontine glioma expands the brainstem rather than the vermis.
